planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Grandiflorum needs room to develop its tiered, horizontal branching without crowding.

directions: One of the oldest named selections of the Japanese snowball form, Grandiflorum carries entirely sterile flower clusters that open as tight green-white domes in mid-spring and swell into dense, rounded balls of pure white florets lined up along the top of each horizontal branch. Because every floret is sterile it sets no fruit, so the plant channels its energy into an especially long, heavy bloom display rather than berries, and the branching stays strongly tiered and layered even without pruning. Dark green, prominently veined summer foliage turns a muted bronze-red in fall before dropping. Thin out only crossing or damaged wood right after flowering to preserve the horizontal branching pattern that gives the shrub its structure.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Rosace flowers most heavily where it gets several hours of direct sun.

directions: Raised in France and later given an RHS Award of Garden Merit, Rosace is a fertile lacecap doublefile whose flat flower clusters open creamy white in late spring and then gradually flush rose-pink to deep red as they age, so a single plant can show both colors on the branch at once by early summer. The sterile ray florets ringing each cluster are noticeably broad and rounded compared with many doublefile selections, giving the flower heads a fuller, more substantial look. Fertile center florets that follow set red fruit ripening to black, and the horizontally tiered branches carry decent burgundy fall color. Prune minimally, right after bloom, to keep the characteristic layered habit intact.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Fujisanensis Doublefile Viburnum (Compact Mount Fuji Form)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Fujisanensis stays noticeably more compact than typical doublefile viburnum and needs less room to mature.

directions: Originally found growing on the slopes of Mount Fuji in Japan, this selection stays considerably more compact and dense than the typical doublefile viburnum, making it a better fit for smaller gardens where the full-size species would quickly outgrow its space. In mid-spring the tiered branches still carry the classic doublefile lacecap flowers, with a flat ring of white sterile florets surrounding tiny fertile ones, followed by red fruit ripening to black against dark green, finely textured foliage. Its tighter, denser branching holds the horizontal, layered silhouette with less sprawl than larger-growing doublefile cultivars. Prune only lightly after flowering to maintain the naturally neat habit.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Nanum Semperflorens Dwarf Doublefile Viburnum (Repeat-Blooming Compact Form)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Nanum Semperflorens is one of the smallest doublefile selections and fits spaces too tight for a standard doublefile viburnum.

directions: A true dwarf form of the doublefile viburnum, Nanum Semperflorens grows as a tight, dense mound rarely reaching more than a few feet tall, in sharp contrast to the large, spreading habit of most doublefile cultivars. True to its name, it produces its small white lacecap flower clusters in a strong spring flush and then continues to open scattered new clusters sporadically through summer, rather than flowering only once. The diminutive scale carries through to its leaves and branching, which stay proportionally smaller and denser than the species. Its compact, repeat-flowering habit makes it useful as a low flowering hedge or foundation planting where a standard doublefile would be far too large.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Chico Kiwi (Early California Fuzzy Kiwifruit Selection)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chico was selected in California and is primarily grown among home orchardists and in regional pollinator plantings alongside Hayward rather than as a major commercial cultivar.

directions: Chico is an older California selection of fuzzy kiwifruit, grown mainly in home and small regional orchards rather than at the scale of Hayward. Like all fuzzy kiwi it is dioecious and needs a compatible vine of the opposite sex nearby for fruit set, and it shares the vigorous twining growth habit that demands a sturdy T-bar or pergola trellis and hard annual winter pruning to keep fruiting wood renewed and manageable. Fruit ripens later in the fall growing season and should be picked while still firm, then finished indoors at room temperature once the seeds inside have darkened. Give it a long, warm, frost-free season, since fuzzy kiwi of any selection struggles to ripen fully in short-season climates.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Kiwifruit Fruit Facts
University of California Cooperative Extension — Kiwifruit Culture
